bibl.title: Deconvolution improves the detection and quantification of spike transmission gain from spike trains

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: how much of what is read as a connection between two neurons is contributed by the firing pattern of each neuron on its own
span.quote: Accurate detection and quantification of spike transmission between neurons is essential for determining neural network mechanisms that govern cognitive functions. Using point process and conductance-based simulations, we found that existing methods for determining neuronal connectivity from spike times are highly affected by burst spiking activity, resulting in over- or underestimation of spike transmission. To improve performance, we developed a mathematical framework for decomposing the cross-correlation between two spike trains. We then devised a deconvolution-based algorithm for removing effects of second-order spike train statistics. Deconvolution removed the effect of burst spiking, improving the estimation of neuronal connectivity yielded by state-of-the-art methods. Application of deconvolution to neuronal data recorded from hippocampal region CA1 of freely-moving mice produced higher estimates of spike transmission, in particular when spike trains exhibited bursts. Deconvolution facilitates the precise construction of complex connectivity maps, opening the door to enhanced understanding of the neural mechanisms underlying brain function.

span.label: method
span.quote: We then devised a deconvolution-based algorithm for removing effects of second-order spike train statistics.

span.label: spike transmission between connected neurons
span.quote: Accurate detection and quantification of spike transmission between neurons is essential for determining neural network mechanisms that govern cognitive functions.

span.label: simulation
span.quote: Using point process and conductance-based simulations, we found that existing methods for determining neuronal connectivity from spike times are highly affected by burst spiking activity, resulting in over- or underestimation of spike transmission.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Because the CCH contains each neuron's auto-correlation convolved with the transmission impulse response, presynaptic bursts inject fast side lobes into the CCH; timescale separation cannot strip them out, so the estimated gain is biased by burstiness rather than by synaptic strength.
span.quote: Hence, even if an optimal estimate of the other inputs is removed, a CCH between two synaptically-connected neurons will still contain contributions from the ACHs of each neuron.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Bursting of the presynaptic neuron produces secondary peaks flanking the causal peak of the CCH, which is the concrete distortion the estimators mistake for transmission.
span.quote: In addition, the CCH exhibited side lobes: secondary peaks with increased counts on both sides of the causal peak, which are due to the bursting activity of the presynaptic neuron.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Deconvolving the two auto-correlation histograms out of the CCH removes the ACH-induced side lobes, leaving a histogram whose causal peak reflects transmission alone before the other-inputs term is subtracted.
span.quote: In a nutshell, the algorithm mitigates the effect of bursting activity by deconvolving the ACHs from the CCH, resulting in a CCH which does not exhibit ACH-induced side lobes

span.label: A CCH CAN BE DESCRIBED AS A SUM OF THREE ELEMENTS: (1) THE CONVOLUTION BETWEEN THE ACH OF NEURON 1 AND THE IMPULSE RESPONSE FROM NEURON 1 TO NEURON 2; (2) THE CONVOLUTION BETWEEN THE ACH OF NEURON 2 AND THE IMPULSE RESPONSE FROM NEURON 2 TO NEURON 1; AND (3) THE CROSS-CORRELATION BETWEEN THE BACKGROUND SPIKE TRAINS, THOSE NOT DUE TO DIRECT CONNECTIVITY BETWEEN THE TWO NEURONS
span.quote: Thus, a CCH can be described as a sum of three elements: (1) the convolution between the ACH of neuron 1 and the impulse response from neuron 1 to neuron 2; (2) the convolution between the ACH of neuron 2 and the impulse response from neuron 2 to neuron 1; and (3) the cross-correlation between the background spike trains, those not due to direct connectivity between the two neurons.

span.label: and the decomposition buys a change of shape: THE LAST EXPRESSION HAS THE CONCEPTUAL BENEFIT OF OPENING THE LOOP, EFFECTIVELY DESCRIBING A FEEDBACK SYSTEM AS A FEEDFORWARD SYSTEM USING AN ARITHMETIC DECOMPOSITION, so that hidden elements can be reconstructed FROM THE CCH USING NUMERICAL METHODS
span.quote: The last expression has the conceptual benefit of opening the loop, effectively describing a feedback system (Fig. 2a ) as a feedforward system using an arithmetic decomposition (Fig. 2e ). Moreover, understanding that the CCH is a sum of three elements allows reconstructing hidden elements, namely the STCs, from the CCH using numerical methods.

span.label: why the field's existing filter cannot work: WHEN ONE OF TWO CONNECTED NEURONS EXHIBITS HIGH-FREQUENCY PERIODICITY OR BURST SPIKING, FAST FEATURES APPEAR IN THE CCH, and THESE FEATURES CANNOT BE DIFFERENTIATED FROM TRANSMITTED SPIKES BY TIMESCALE SEPARATION
span.quote: When one of two connected neurons exhibits high-frequency periodicity or burst spiking, fast features appear in the CCH 22 , 23 . These features cannot be differentiated from transmitted spikes by timescale separation. Thus, even when timescale separation methods are used, transmitted spikes cannot be fully differentiated from non-transmission patterns such as burst spiking activity.

span.label: and the same synapse transmits differently depending on the background: WEAKER EPSPs (0.2-1 mV) COULD INDUCE CONSISTENT SPIKING WHEN NOISE WAS SUFFICIENTLY HIGH, and THE uEPSP MAGNITUDE REQUIRED TO GENERATE A FIXED rSTG DECREASED MONOTONICALLY WITH the noise
span.quote: While even relatively-large EPSPs fail to produce postsynaptic spikes in the lack of membrane potential variability, weaker EPSPs (0.2–1 mV) could induce consistent spiking when noise was sufficiently high. Moreover, the uEPSP magnitude required to generate a fixed rSTG decreased monotonically with σ (Fig. 1b , bottom inset). Thus, EPSP magnitude alone does not suffice for estimating spike transmission.

span.label: The method assumes fixed auto-correlations and connectivity over time, so it cannot track time-dependent changes in spike transmission.
span.quote: As is, the deconvolution approach presented here (as well as the timescale separation methods employed) does not take into account time-dependent changes in the auto-correlation (e.g., of bursting activity) and cannot estimate time-dependent changes of spike transmission.

span.label: The point-process simulations covered only feedforward two-neuron pairs and may miss features of larger reciprocally connected networks.
span.quote: However, the point process simulations were limited to two-neuron “networks” with feedforward connectivity and may not exhibit other features, produced in larger-scale networks with reciprocally-connected neurons.

span.label: The mathematical framework assumes linear time-invariant spike transmission, an assumption incompatible with real neuronal refractoriness.
span.quote: Linearity is incompatible with neuronal refractoriness, and is assumed for mathematical simplicity.

span.label: In the real-neuron dataset there is no ground truth for the true spike transmission gain.
span.quote: In contrast to simulations, rSTGs are of course unknown for the real neuronal data.

span.label: THE UNDERLYING ASSUMPTION WAS THAT THE ACHs AND CONNECTIVITY STRENGTHS ARE FIXED OVER TIME, and AS IS, THE DECONVOLUTION APPROACH PRESENTED HERE (AS WELL AS THE TIMESCALE SEPARATION METHODS EMPLOYED) DOES NOT TAKE INTO ACCOUNT TIME-DEPENDENT CHANGES IN THE AUTO-CORRELATION AND CANNOT ESTIMATE TIME-DEPENDENT CHANGES OF SPIKE TRANSMISSION
span.quote: Estimates of STG/PSP yielded by all methods employed (tails, jitter, median, GLMCC, and CoNNECT) were averaged over time and spike patterns. The underlying assumption was that the ACHs and connectivity strengths are fixed over time. However, previous studies have shown that the postsynaptic effect of a presynaptic spike may depend on the presynaptic inter-spike interval 3 , 10 , 11 and on other parameters 32 , 47 . In vitro work showed that synaptic transmission can exhibit short-term plasticity, where the EPSP magnitude in a postsynaptic neuron is modified according to the order and timing of presynaptic spikes 48 . In some cases, EPSP magnitude decreased over consecutive spikes, and in other cases consecutive spikes caused facilitation of EPSP magnitude 3 , 49 . Consistent with the in vitro work, spike transmission estimates derived from the CCH in vivo were distinct when CCHs were computed using the first, second, or third spike in a presynaptic burst 21 , 32 , 50 , 51 . Other in vivo studies used trial-averaging and time-resolved cross-correlation measures, showing that spike-to-spike correlations depend on the time lag relative to a stimulus or an action 32 , 47 , 52 . As is, the deconvolution approach presented here (as well as the timescale separation methods employed) does not take into account time-dependent changes in the auto-correlation (e.g., of bursting activity) and cannot estimate time-dependent changes of spike transmission.

span.label: the decomposition is an approximation with a stated domain - THE APPROXIMATION IS VALID AS LONG AS THE PRODUCT OF THE TWO STGs (I.E., THE LOOP GAIN) IS SMALL
span.quote: The approximation is valid as long as the product of the two STGs (i.e., the loop gain) is small.

span.label: THE POINT PROCESS SIMULATIONS WERE LIMITED TO TWO-NEURON NETWORKS WITH FEEDFORWARD CONNECTIVITY AND MAY NOT EXHIBIT OTHER FEATURES, PRODUCED IN LARGER-SCALE NETWORKS WITH RECIPROCALLY-CONNECTED NEURONS
span.quote: However, the point process simulations were limited to two-neuron “networks” with feedforward connectivity and may not exhibit other features, produced in larger-scale networks with reciprocally-connected neurons.

span.label: IN CONTRAST TO SIMULATIONS, rSTGs ARE OF COURSE UNKNOWN FOR THE REAL NEURONAL DATA, so the real-data test is indirect - the contribution was tested BY MEASURING THE eSTG RATIO (WITHOUT AND WITH DECONVOLUTION) AS A FUNCTION OF THE BURST INDEX
span.quote: In contrast to simulations, rSTGs are of course unknown for the real neuronal data. Therefore, we tested the contribution of deconvolution by measuring the eSTG ratio (without and with deconvolution) as a function of the burst index.

span.label: THE ESTIMATES YIELDED BY THE PSP-BASED METHODS CANNOT BE GAUGED DIRECTLY IN THE CASE OF THE SYNTHETIC CCH, SINCE NO GROUND TRUTH FOR PSP EXISTS IN THE POINT PROCESS SIMULATIONS - two of the five methods report in units the simulation cannot produce
span.quote: While the tails, jitter, and median filtering methods yield estimates of effective connectivity measured as gain (STG; Fig. 1 ), the GLMCC and CoNNECT methods produce estimates in units of mV (PSP). The estimates yielded by the PSP-based methods cannot be gauged directly in the case of the synthetic CCH depicted in Fig. 3c , since no ground truth for PSP exists in the point process simulations.

span.label: the real-data analysis keeps a sixth of the pairs - ONLY PYR-TO-INT PAIRS WITH A CONSISTENT MONOSYNAPTIC CCH PEAK, IN WHICH THE PYR EXHIBITED A NON-NEGATIVE BURST INDEX, WERE ANALYZED (1274/7991 PAIRS)
span.quote: Only PYR-to-INT pairs with a consistent monosynaptic CCH peak ( p < 0.001, Poisson test), in which the PYR exhibited a non-negative burst index, were analyzed (1274/7991 pairs).

span.label: the tool does not help one of the five methods - WITH THE EXCEPTION OF CoNNECT, DECONVOLUTION REDUCED THE EFFECT OF BURSTING FOR ALL METHODS
span.quote: With the exception of CoNNECT, deconvolution reduced the effect of bursting for all methods

span.label: and the measurement it improves is correlative in the first place - MOST CCH APPLICATIONS EMPLOY SPONTANEOUS SPIKING, AND ARE THEREFORE CORRELATIVE MEASUREMENTS WHICH CANNOT DIFFERENTIATE CAUSAL TRANSMISSION FROM NON-CAUSAL SPIKE PATTERNS
span.quote: However, most CCH applications employ spontaneous spiking, and are therefore correlative measurements which cannot differentiate causal transmission from non-causal spike patterns. For example, firing of two cells may be co-modulated by another source such as visual input or a third neuron, causing the two cells to fire in synchrony 12 . Thus, the CCH is influenced not only by spike transmission properties but also by co-modulation of the pre- and postsynaptic trains

span.label: the move that OPENS THE LOOP - EFFECTIVELY DESCRIBING A FEEDBACK SYSTEM AS A FEEDFORWARD SYSTEM USING AN ARITHMETIC DECOMPOSITION, which ALLOWS RECONSTRUCTING HIDDEN ELEMENTS, NAMELY THE STCs, FROM THE CCH USING NUMERICAL METHODS
span.quote: The last expression has the conceptual benefit of opening the loop, effectively describing a feedback system (Fig. 2a ) as a feedforward system using an arithmetic decomposition (Fig. 2e ). Moreover, understanding that the CCH is a sum of three elements allows reconstructing hidden elements, namely the STCs, from the CCH using numerical methods.

span.label: the spike transmission curve defined as an impulse response, so that THE CCH IS IDENTICAL TO THE CONVOLUTION BETWEEN THE ACH OF NEURON 1 AND THE STC
span.quote: Thus, a CCH can be described as a sum of three elements: (1) the convolution between the ACH of neuron 1 and the impulse response from neuron 1 to neuron 2; (2) the convolution between the ACH of neuron 2 and the impulse response from neuron 2 to neuron 1; and (3) the cross-correlation between the background spike trains, those not due to direct connectivity between the two neurons.

span.label: the estimator run against a simulation in which the connection strength was IDENTICAL for every pair and only burstiness varied
span.quote: Although E-to-I connection strengths were the same for all pairs, median filtering without deconvolution yielded eSTGs which were highly affected by the BF ( ρ = −0.68, p < 0.001, permutation test; Fig. 5e ). In contrast, median filtering with deconvolution produced eSTGs that were not correlated with burstiness

span.label: the whole method first validated on a case with a known answer and no complications
span.quote: Considering all non-zero rSTG values, the mean eSTG error (eSTG–rSTG)/rSTG, was 2.5% (456 spike train pairs with non-zero rSTG; smaller than 5%, p < 0.05, one-tailed Wilcoxon’s signed-rank test; Fig. 1d ). Thus, the STG estimated from the CCH between spike trains closely matches the real spike transmission gain.

span.label: the naive definition of the quantity replaced by a corrected one
span.quote: However, such computation is flawed since the addition of transmitted spikes occasionally decimates spontaneous (noise-induced) spikes. In the case of a LIF model with an absolute refractory period ARP 2 and time step Δ t , the exact rSTG is obtained by multiplying the naive ratio by a correction factor that scales the firing rate difference by the fraction of non-occupied bins

span.label: the two-cell result repeated in hundred-neuron conductance-based networks with reciprocal connections
span.quote: However, the point process simulations were limited to two-neuron “networks” with feedforward connectivity and may not exhibit other features, produced in larger-scale networks with reciprocally-connected neurons.

span.label: the improvement measured as error against ground truth, not only as a change in the estimate
span.quote: We found that deconvolution reduced the MSE for all STG-based methods ( p < 0.001; Wilcoxon’s paired signed-rank test; Fig. 4h ). Of the three STG-based methods, median filtering with deconvolution had the lowest MSE (1.27 × 10 −5 ). Median without deconvolution and jitter with deconvolution had the second and third lowest MSEs, respectively (median: 2.73 × 10 −5 ; jitter with deconvolution: 3.48 × 10 −5 ; jitter: 5.34 × 10 −5 ). Thus, deconvolution reduced the errors approximately two-fold.

span.label: the real-data effect tested as a FUNCTION of burst index rather than as a mean shift
span.quote: Over 1274 pairs, eSTG ratios exhibited a negative correlation with burst indices ( ρ = −0.348; p < 0.001, permutation test; Fig. 6g ). Furthermore, most eSTG ratios were smaller than one (median: 0.88; p < 0.001, Wilcoxon’s signed-rank test; Fig. 6g ). The negative correlation between eSTG ratio and burst index in real neuronal data, and the fact that most eSTG ratios are smaller than one, are consistent with the controlled simulations

span.label: STG → spike transmission probability
span.note: FOUR NAMES FOR ONE CONSTRUCT, EACH WITH ITS OWN CITATION, IN ONE SENTENCE: the spike transmission gain (STG) has been called “effectiveness” [33], “asynchronous gain” [34], “synaptic efficacy” [11] and “spike transmission probability” by previous studies. The relation is ONE-TO-FOUR and the concept_edges form is binary, so splitting it into four `renamed-across-fields` edges would give each name a partner and lose the set - which is the only part that matters, because THE POINT IS THAT THERE ARE FOUR. A literature search on any one name misses the other three, and nothing in the layer records that they are the same measure. The author had to interrupt a methods section to say so, which is where this kind of fact usually lives and why it usually travels nowhere.
span.quote: Previous studies have referred to the STG using various other names: “effectiveness” 33 , “asynchronous gain” 34 , “synaptic efficacy” 11 , and “spike transmission probability”

span.label: ONE QUANTITY, FIVE NAMES, AND THE PAPER LISTS THEM WITH CITATIONS: PREVIOUS STUDIES HAVE REFERRED TO THE STG USING VARIOUS OTHER NAMES: “EFFECTIVENESS”, “ASYNCHRONOUS GAIN”, “SYNAPTIC EFFICACY”, AND “SPIKE TRANSMISSION PROBABILITY”. A `renamed-across-fields` edge that the corpus usually has to infer, printed in the source
span.quote: Previous studies have referred to the STG using various other names: “effectiveness” 33 , “asynchronous gain” 34 , “synaptic efficacy” 11 , and “spike transmission probability”

span.label: THREE PUBLISHED ESTIMATORS OF THE SAME QUANTITY, ON THE SAME DATA, WITH A KNOWN ANSWER, DISAGREE FROM 58% TO 133%: THE TAILS PREDICTOR OVERESTIMATED THE rSTG (133%), AND THE JITTER AND MEDIAN PREDICTORS UNDERESTIMATED IT (JITTER: 58%; MEDIAN FILTERING: 70%). Not noise - the sign of the error is a property of the estimator
span.quote: The tails predictor overestimated the rSTG (eSTG = 0.053, 133%; Fig. 3d ), and the jitter and median predictors underestimated the rSTG (jitter: 0.023, 58%; median filtering: 0.028, 70%). Thus, when burst spiking activity is present, the tails, jitter, and median methods fail to produce an accurate eSTG.

span.label: AND THE NUMBER MOVES WITH A PROPERTY THAT IS NOT THE CONNECTION: ALTHOUGH E-TO-I CONNECTION STRENGTHS WERE THE SAME FOR ALL PAIRS, MEDIAN FILTERING WITHOUT DECONVOLUTION YIELDED eSTGs WHICH WERE HIGHLY AFFECTED BY THE BF. Identical ground truth, and the measurement varies with how the presynaptic cell happens to fire
span.quote: Although E-to-I connection strengths were the same for all pairs, median filtering without deconvolution yielded eSTGs which were highly affected by the BF ( ρ = −0.68, p < 0.001, permutation test; Fig. 5e ). In contrast, median filtering with deconvolution produced eSTGs that were not correlated with burstiness

span.label: stated by the authors as the general form: EVEN WHEN CONNECTIONS HAVE FIXED STRENGTHS, THE eSTGs DEPEND ON BURST SPIKING ACTIVITY
span.quote: Thus, even when connections have fixed strengths, the eSTGs depend on burst spiking activity. However, dependency is minimized using deconvolution.

span.label: THE FIELD'S SHARED ASSUMPTION, WRITTEN OUT: AN UNDERLYING ASSUMPTION IN THESE APPROACHES IS THAT WHILE DIRECT CONNECTIONS EXHIBIT FAST TRANSIENTS IN THE CCH, INDIRECT SOURCES PRODUCE SLOWER FLUCTUATIONS - the whole timescale-separation family rests on it
span.quote: An underlying assumption in these approaches is that while direct connections exhibit fast transients in the CCH, indirect sources produce slower fluctuations. Based on this assumption, timescale separation can be used to detect and estimate synaptic connectivity, differentiating between fast transients (which are presumably due to direct connectivity), and slower fluctuations (which are presumably due to other sources).

span.label: and then broken by a case it does not cover: WHEN ONE OF TWO CONNECTED NEURONS EXHIBITS HIGH-FREQUENCY PERIODICITY OR BURST SPIKING, FAST FEATURES APPEAR IN THE CCH, and THESE FEATURES CANNOT BE DIFFERENTIATED FROM TRANSMITTED SPIKES BY TIMESCALE SEPARATION
span.quote: When one of two connected neurons exhibits high-frequency periodicity or burst spiking, fast features appear in the CCH 22 , 23 . These features cannot be differentiated from transmitted spikes by timescale separation. Thus, even when timescale separation methods are used, transmitted spikes cannot be fully differentiated from non-transmission patterns such as burst spiking activity.

span.label: TWO OF THE FIVE METHODS REPORT IN UNITS THE GROUND TRUTH DOES NOT HAVE: THE TAILS, JITTER, AND MEDIAN FILTERING METHODS YIELD ESTIMATES MEASURED AS GAIN, THE GLMCC AND CoNNECT METHODS PRODUCE ESTIMATES IN UNITS OF mV, and THE ESTIMATES YIELDED BY THE PSP-BASED METHODS CANNOT BE GAUGED DIRECTLY, SINCE NO GROUND TRUTH FOR PSP EXISTS IN THE POINT PROCESS SIMULATIONS
span.quote: While the tails, jitter, and median filtering methods yield estimates of effective connectivity measured as gain (STG; Fig. 1 ), the GLMCC and CoNNECT methods produce estimates in units of mV (PSP). The estimates yielded by the PSP-based methods cannot be gauged directly in the case of the synthetic CCH depicted in Fig. 3c , since no ground truth for PSP exists in the point process simulations.

span.label: THE MEASUREMENT IS CORRELATIVE AND THE PAPER SAYS SO: MOST CCH APPLICATIONS EMPLOY SPONTANEOUS SPIKING, AND ARE THEREFORE CORRELATIVE MEASUREMENTS WHICH CANNOT DIFFERENTIATE CAUSAL TRANSMISSION FROM NON-CAUSAL SPIKE PATTERNS - every `causes` edge built on a CCH inherits this
span.quote: However, most CCH applications employ spontaneous spiking, and are therefore correlative measurements which cannot differentiate causal transmission from non-causal spike patterns. For example, firing of two cells may be co-modulated by another source such as visual input or a third neuron, causing the two cells to fire in synchrony 12 . Thus, the CCH is influenced not only by spike transmission properties but also by co-modulation of the pre- and postsynaptic trains

span.quote: Thus, EPSP magnitude alone is insufficient for determining whether a postsynaptic neuron will fire following a presynaptic spike, thereby allowing information to pass on to other cells.

span.label: and the missing variable is named and measured: WHILE EVEN RELATIVELY-LARGE EPSPs FAIL TO PRODUCE POSTSYNAPTIC SPIKES IN THE LACK OF MEMBRANE POTENTIAL VARIABILITY, WEAKER EPSPs (0.2-1 mV) COULD INDUCE CONSISTENT SPIKING WHEN NOISE WAS SUFFICIENTLY HIGH. The same synapse, opposite outcomes, decided by the background

Moreover, the uEPSP magnitude required to generate a fixed rSTG decreased monotonically with σ (Fig. 1b , bottom inset). Thus, EPSP magnitude alone does not suffice for estimating spike transmission.

span.label: THE OBVIOUS DEFINITION OF THE GROUND TRUTH IS WRONG, AND THE PAPER DERIVES THE CORRECTION: SUCH COMPUTATION IS FLAWED SINCE THE ADDITION OF TRANSMITTED SPIKES OCCASIONALLY DECIMATES SPONTANEOUS (NOISE-INDUCED) SPIKES - THE EXACT rSTG IS OBTAINED BY MULTIPLYING THE NAIVE RATIO BY A CORRECTION FACTOR THAT SCALES THE FIRING RATE DIFFERENCE BY THE FRACTION OF NON-OCCUPIED BINS

In the case of a LIF model with an absolute refractory period ARP 2 and time step Δ t , the exact rSTG is obtained by multiplying the naive ratio by a correction factor that scales the firing rate difference by the fraction of non-occupied bins

span.quote: Estimates of STG/PSP yielded by all methods employed (tails, jitter, median, GLMCC, and CoNNECT) were averaged over time and spike patterns. The underlying assumption was that the ACHs and connectivity strengths are fixed over time. However, previous studies have shown that the postsynaptic effect of a presynaptic spike may depend on the presynaptic inter-spike interval 3 , 10 , 11 and on other parameters 32 , 47 . In vitro work showed that synaptic transmission can exhibit short-term plasticity, where the EPSP magnitude in a postsynaptic neuron is modified according to the order and timing of presynaptic spikes 48 . In some cases, EPSP magnitude decreased over consecutive spikes, and in other cases consecutive spikes caused facilitation of EPSP magnitude 3 , 49 . Consistent with the in vitro work, spike transmission estimates derived from the CCH in vivo were distinct when CCHs were computed using the first, second, or third spike in a presynaptic burst 21 , 32 , 50 , 51 . Other in vivo studies used trial-averaging and time-resolved cross-correlation measures, showing that spike-to-spike correlations depend on the time lag relative to a stimulus or an action 32 , 47 , 52 . As is, the deconvolution approach presented here (as well as the timescale separation methods employed) does not take into account time-dependent changes in the auto-correlation (e.g., of bursting activity) and cannot estimate time-dependent changes of spike transmission.

span.label: AN APPROXIMATION WITH ITS DOMAIN PRINTED: THE APPROXIMATION IS VALID AS LONG AS THE PRODUCT OF THE TWO STGs (I.E., THE LOOP GAIN) IS SMALL
span.quote: The approximation is valid as long as the product of the two STGs (i.e., the loop gain) is small.

span.label: AND THE REAL DATA HAS NO GROUND TRUTH AT ALL: IN CONTRAST TO SIMULATIONS, rSTGs ARE OF COURSE UNKNOWN FOR THE REAL NEURONAL DATA - so the real-data claim is a consistency check against the simulations, not a measurement of accuracy
span.quote: In contrast to simulations, rSTGs are of course unknown for the real neuronal data. Therefore, we tested the contribution of deconvolution by measuring the eSTG ratio (without and with deconvolution) as a function of the burst index.

span.label: a negative reported about the authors' own tool: WITH THE EXCEPTION OF CoNNECT, DECONVOLUTION REDUCED THE EFFECT OF BURSTING FOR ALL METHODS
span.quote: With the exception of CoNNECT, deconvolution reduced the effect of bursting for all methods

span.label: THE METHOD WAS CHOSEN ON TWO CRITERIA AND ONE OF THEM IS SPEED: OF THE STG-BASED METHODS, MEDIAN FILTERING YIELDED THE BEST PERFORMANCE, and its runtime was THREE TO FOUR ORDERS OF MAGNITUDE FASTER THAN THE RUNTIME OF PSP-BASED METHODS
span.quote: To focus on the contribution of deconvolution, we chose to use a single timescale separation method from this point onward. Of the STG-based methods, median filtering yielded the best performance, with respect to both quantification (Fig. 4h ) and detection (Fig. 4t ). Run times were tested on synthetic spike trains with firing rates of 2 and 8 spk/s, recorded over 5 h. The median [IQR] runtime of median filtering was 0.65 [0.64 0.67] ms, three to four orders of magnitude faster than the runtime of PSP-based methods (GLMCC: 3.72 [2.88 4.55] s; CoNNECT: 1.62 [1.54 1.69] s). These runtimes and performance made median filtering our method of choice for evaluating the contribution of deconvolution in biophysical simulations

span.label: the improvement, in the units of the thing being estimated: DECONVOLUTION REDUCED THE MSE FOR ALL STG-BASED METHODS, approximately TWO-FOLD
span.quote: We found that deconvolution reduced the MSE for all STG-based methods ( p < 0.001; Wilcoxon’s paired signed-rank test; Fig. 4h ). Of the three STG-based methods, median filtering with deconvolution had the lowest MSE (1.27 × 10 −5 ). Median without deconvolution and jitter with deconvolution had the second and third lowest MSEs, respectively (median: 2.73 × 10 −5 ; jitter with deconvolution: 3.48 × 10 −5 ; jitter: 5.34 × 10 −5 ). span.quote: Estimates of STG/PSP yielded by all methods employed (tails, jitter, median, GLMCC, and CoNNECT) were averaged over time and spike patterns. However, previous studies have shown that the postsynaptic effect of a presynaptic spike may depend on the presynaptic inter-spike interval 3 , 10 , 11 and on other parameters 32 , 47 . In vitro work showed that synaptic transmission can exhibit short-term plasticity, where the EPSP magnitude in a postsynaptic neuron is modified according to the order and timing of presynaptic spikes 48 . In some cases, EPSP magnitude decreased over consecutive spikes, and in other cases consecutive spikes caused facilitation of EPSP magnitude 3 , 49 .
